subject: Pathology
title: Cell Injury & Patterns of Tissue Necrosis
preview: The pattern of necrosis reflects mechanism and tissue context, providing strong pathology examination clues.

sections.title: Coagulative versus liquefactive
points: Coagulative: tissue outlines persist transiently after ischemic injury in many solid organs.
Liquefactive: enzymatic digestion dominates, as in brain infarction and abscess formation.

sections.title: Caseous and fat necrosis
points: Caseous: amorphous granular debris in granulomatous inflammation, classically associated with tuberculosis but not unique to it.
Fat necrosis: lipase-related destruction in pancreatitis or trauma can cause calcium soap formation (saponification).

sections.title: Fibrinoid vascular injury
points: Fibrinoid change in vessel walls reflects marked vascular injury with plasma-protein/fibrin-related deposition and can occur in some immune-mediated vasculitides.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Do not assume every infarct is coagulative: brain ischemia is the classic exception.

quickRevision: Coagulative necrosis commonly follows ischemia in solid organs outside the central nervous system.
Liquefactive necrosis is characteristic of cerebral infarction and many suppurative infections.
Caseous, fat and fibrinoid necrosis each have distinct inflammatory or metabolic associations.

quiz.question: Liquefactive necrosis is classically associated with what?
quiz.explanation: Cerebral infarction. • Liquefactive Necrosis: Complete digestion of dead cells transforming tissue into a liquid viscous mass.
